cards.title: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders

depth.text: Goldman is restricting **AI coding tools** to engineers after **traders and bankers** used them at work

An **October update** restricts Anthropic's **Claude Code** and Microsoft's GitHub to engineers; traders had used them to monitor client flows and model market moves. Goldman and Morgan Stanley are **lead underwriters** on Anthropic's IPO.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say security and compliance risks justify the cutoff; others want nontechnical staff to keep access, with engineering building safer tools. Some separately speculate about billing or an operational loss.

comments.text: People are giving all kinds of explanations here why Goldman is doing this, but they are not addressing what the article (implicitly) says: operating coding agents on the primary machines of finance professionals runs directly into the lethal trifecta. It's as simple as that. You cannot have semi-unattended agents running on the same workstations that have access to client/trade/prop information…

At our org they have been clawing back Claude access because of chronic billing overages. Budgets are tight and consumption billing models are being stamped down on everywhere. Anthropic sales can not offer us any sort of normalized billing rate. Gemini is swooping in because they offer flat consistent billing and handle overages through throttling access to higher models. For 90% of the…
The most interesting part of this announcement is the timing. GS is leading Anthropic's IPO, what motivated them to announce this a few weeks before trading starts?

Regardless of tech tool, non-tech writing POCs they try to force tech to get into production is a timeless story. LLM just allows people to get there faster, with less knowledge of coding.. which leads to the actual problem I think. Banks have a ton of legal/compliance/reglatory/reputational concerns about application access/entitleements, data privacy, data licensing, granular data entitlements…

Goldman is very unlikely to have decided proactively to cut off traders access, and it's much more likely there was an operational loss. What kind of loss? I don't know but consider: 1) Claude Code is only being taken away from traders. 2) Only traders have permission to send orders to the market and book client trades. 3) Claude code would probably have been running as the trader, under their…

cards.title: Llama-modchip: 284B DeepSeek on 64GB RAM, no GPU

depth.text: someone got a **284B DeepSeek model** running on **64GB of RAM** with no GPU

The project compresses the checkpoint from 76.87 GiB to **56.56 GiB**, then fits the model and a 256K KV cache in RAM with **zero swap**. It reports 44.4 tok/s for prompt processing and 9.1–14.7 tok/s for generation on a 16-core Zen 5.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters see clever optimizations making local AI practical; skeptics say aggressive quantization may hurt quality and question whether the repo adds much beyond llama.cpp.

comments.text: The floor for a functional local AI system keeps getting lower, dispite ram and GPU prices continuing to go up. An E5 workstation with lots of threads, $300 of RAM and at least $100 of GPU gets you something that can do >100tok/s+ prompt processing, and ~20tok/s output with Qwen3.8-flash-next:IQ3_S. Toss a $500 GPU in there, and it goes from barely usable to pleasingly performant. For less than…

Something to keep in mind with aggressive quantisation, is that it's been empirically proven [1] that (1) quantisation has non-linear performance behaviour, and (2) generally the peak size-to-performance ratio occurs at 4-bit; anything lower and you will see significant reduction in performance. Also, I've been playing with speech models for the past 2 years, and for me anything below 8-bit is a…

To put this on perspective, consider that with 128GB of unified RAM it can run even fast : https://x.com/antirez/status/2119392658661749175
Like, coding-agent acceptably fast. See later in the reply for the prefill at ~300 t/s but can go even faster for larger prefills.

Stupid question, but does this AI-generated repo actually _do_ anything? Comparing it on Nemotron, it runs just about the same as plain old llama.cpp on the cpu (except prefill seems much faster). I don't see an option to set up DeepSeek in "modchip setup", so I haven't tested that one yet. Edit: this is on a Ryzen 7945hx 16-core Zen 4 + 96 gb DDR5.
The quantization is probably the most important thing to know and its not clear at all from the dense word salad

cards.title: Writing as a thinking tool

depth.text: writing can help people **work out what they think**, not just **explain it** to someone else

cards.camps: Two camps: some see AI writing as a shortcut around the author's thinking; others use an LLM as a dialog partner, but say to ask it for explanations and check its work with demos.
entities: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance

comments.text: When I had started my PhD, I thought the writing part of a paper was just the last thing I needed to do to summarize my results, like a boring epilogue to the more exciting science. What surprised me was how much of the scientific process relied on my ability to convey my ideas to someone else. And to be able to do that you need clarity of mind, you need to have worked through multiple drafts to…

This is true for designing, too. I see a lot of people saying Figma is dead because you can prototype directly; for novel UX problems the act of designing — of putting ideas together, assembling a component, even getting good data into a design — is where a lot of my thinking and insights develop. The brain work plus the craft work, the tight loop between thinking and creating is so critical for…

Writing code (Programming) is a thinking tool too. When you are writing code manually, actually you are thinking about what you are doing, what you will build actually, what are your or users' real requirements, etc.

Most of my projects are born out of scribbles on paper, system diagrams with boxes and little arrows to try to describe the system I want to build or my thought process written down like in this post. When I get it on paper and everything feels right I start creating the codebase but I have to get it down first, feels like I remember it more after I save my thoughts to external paper storage.

I always carry a small Moleskine notebook, the pocket-sized hardcover with grid paper, for notes, thoughts, and whatever else comes to mind during the day. Each page is numbered, and I continue the numbering as I move from one notebook to the next. This allows quick reference to past ideas, thoughts, or notes I may have in an older notebook, or even a few pages back. It is the primary way I get…

cards.title: Petered

depth.text: someone argues people **promoted past competence** may do **dirty work** to save their careers

In *Making a Career in Dictatorship*, Gläßel and Scharpf say career pressure can push people to take on **morally contentious tasks** or **sabotage superiors** to regain competitiveness. The essay asks whether talk of imposter syndrome helps obscure **actual imposters** who hide what they do behind busyness.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the Peter Principle oversimplifies promotions because higher roles require different skills; others say people can advance past their abilities and then protect themselves through relationships or political moves.

comments.text: <“A-people hire A-people, B-people hire C-people”> I didn't go into management because I didn't think circumstances were stable enough. I did see four co-workers go up the ladder, with disastrous results. Two of them I tried to warn, the other two would have been a waste of time to warn. By the time I retired, two had been fired, one drank himself into a coma, then passed away. The fourth is…

I think the Peter Principle addresses a good point, but misses a critical one: the hierarchy itself. Obviously, a manager requires different skills than an engineer, so why should a good engineer be a good manager? This holds the other way round: a good manager is not particularly likely to be a good engineer. Both is fine, these are just different jobs. However, the problem is that the manager…

After they’ve been promoted to their level of incompetence, they lean in very hard on relationships to survive. Organizations where they get away with this are miserable to work for, and their influence ensures nothing merit-related ever happens again. Literally the source of the famous expression “A-people hire A-people, B-people hire C-people”.

It's easier to remember that in some organizations, it's about what you can do. In others, it's about who you know. But when it comes to internal promotions: it's a mix of both, and promoting people who are likely to boost your own career is an obvious choice. When someone incompetent is promoted, people below them see their incompetence. However, the people above the promoter only see the…

I find the logic behind the principle itself buggy as it assumes that people will not improve in what they do. Even if one gets promoted close to his or her level of incompetence, it doesn’t mean that he can’t become more knowledgeable while making experience. That by the way is almost always the case, unless you reach your hard limit (eg QI or something), then you should not get further promoted…

cards.title: Making any integer with four 2s (2025)

depth.text: someone used nested square roots to make **any natural number** from **exactly four 2s**
Paul Dirac's general solution combines **nested square roots** with **base-2 logarithms**. The article gets to four 2s by replacing one digit with √(2+2).

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters call square roots or writing 22 cheating; the article says its square-root fix fits the puzzle's rules.

comments.text: It’s true cheating, but if you assume the Peano axioms, you can write any integer with one zero without having to resort to complex functions such as √. For example (if I didn’t miscount the S-es or parentheses), S(S(S(S(S(S(S(0)))))))) = 7

i know everyone plays with their own rules, but from my perspective, a square root spends a 2 - it's not an operator like + or ! . there's an implicit "2" since you could also take the cube root or fourth root

there is a related problem (inspired by an interview questions from ITA software, a part of Google now) that asks to find the smallest positive integer that cannot be expressed using a digit K (in [2,9]) N times in an expression that involves the four basic arithmetic operations and the parentheses: +, -, *, /, (, and ). to make the problem more interesting, the list of operations can be extended…
22 is cheating because 22 = 2*10+2 is arbitrary in base 10. If you write 22 in some base, you have to write the base, and that's an extra number.
Popular last year (368 points, 165 comments) https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43145753

cards.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"

depth.text: a new **coding test** shows AI agents often trust **imagined grader expectations** over changed instructions

The team changed instructions or starting code in **89 DeepSWE tasks**, and the score spread widened from 20.9 to **48.3 points** across 15 configurations. They also found seven models reasoned about gaming a **self-reported memory check**, while most failed an independent live-record check.
data: models that reasoned explicitly about gaming

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the results show familiar coding scores overstate real ability; others say the task mutations may not reflect real-world work, or that lower scores still leave models useful.

cards.title: The Components of Agent Memory

depth.text: Anthropic says Claude can **revisit old logs** between sessions to **fix its memories**

Claude’s “dreaming” checks saved notes against old transcripts: in a Pokémon run, it **corrected a wrong PokéCenter location** and eventually reached Cerulean City. In a document test, **wiki plus search** raised the **aggregate score** from 54% to 61%, versus 53% for search alone.

cards.camps: Two camps: Anthropic presents memory review as useful; commenters argue it cannot make models learn continuously, while others object to the “dreaming” label.

comments.text: Interesting article to read but by defining memory as a prediction about future needs they are side stepping the real problem that these models cannot learn continuously i.e. update their weights. Opus 5.5s real memory , experience and knowledge is set in stone no amount of markdown tricks will change that. This is a better research direction I feel…

So far I've turned off automatic memory creation in every harness I've used. Claude Code sometimes creates some anyway, and I probably delete 95% of them. The memories it creates are almost always relevant only to the specific task that it is currently working on. If it's a task I'll need to do again, then yeah, maybe that's useful. But that isn't the case most of the time, so I delete them to…

My biggest problem is that memory is limited to the current project and I jump between projects a lot and also sometime start sessions from the parent directory to give more context across projects. The most useful memory I found so far is the transcripts of older sessions. And not only in one agent but also across agents (like cursor and claude). And also not limited to the current project…

Not sure it's explained here but from the graph (fig. 10) it looks like wiki + search beats dreaming, and that dreaming adds only marginal gains to the wiki + search configuration. I'm assuming search is much cheaper than dreaming (though maybe it depends on the time scale?) so that sounds pretty important.

Concepts made for humans should not be used for machines unless it’s really the same process. Clearly Claud doesn’t rest and doesn’t balance hormones and other chemicals when it’s not thinking. Just because one element of dreaming relates to information organization, organizing information isn’t dreaming. cards.title: Notes on San Marino

depth.text: someone traces how **San Marino** **kept its independence** despite pressure from much larger neighbours

The article says the official **301 founding date** is highly suspect; the first good evidence is an **885 AD church ruling** about the monastery’s separation from the Bishop of Rimini’s lands. It credits repeated **diplomatic deals**, adaptability, and luck for helping San Marino survive stronger powers.

glossary.coding agent: An AI tool that can help write or change code, often by using other tools.
glossary.client trading flows: Information about clients' trades and how much is moving through the market.
glossary.information barriers: Rules that keep sensitive information from passing between groups, such as bankers and traders.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.quantization: A way to make a model use less computing power by representing its internal numbers less precisely.
glossary.MoE: Mixture of Experts: a model with many specialist parts that sends each piece of text to only a few of them.
glossary.prefill: The part of an AI request where it reads the prompt and earlier conversation before writing its answer.
glossary.KV cache: A store of earlier model calculations that it can reuse instead of doing them again.
glossary.tok/s: Tokens per second: a rough measure of how quickly an AI produces text.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.ASI: Artificial Superintelligence: a hypothetical AI far more capable than people across a wide range of tasks.
glossary.foreign intelligence effort: An effort by people working for another country to secretly gather information.
glossary.outside independent counsel: A lawyer from outside the company brought in to help review a matter.
glossary.BASH: Bourne Again SHell: a program that runs written commands, often to automate computer tasks.
glossary.idle RAM: RAM a computer appears not to need at the moment, though people can disagree about what counts as unused.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory: the working memory a computer uses while running things.
glossary.filesystem cache: A place in memory where a computer keeps file information so it can get to it faster next time.
glossary.DDoS: Distributed denial-of-service: an attack that floods a service with traffic so people can't use it.
glossary.CTO: Chief technology officer: the person responsible for a company's technology work.
glossary.FSD: Full Self-Driving: Tesla's name for driving software that, as a commenter notes, still needs a human driver to supervise it.
glossary.vertical integration: A company handling more steps of making or selling its products itself, instead of relying on other companies.
glossary.Robotaxi: A taxi service using cars intended to drive themselves, rather than a human taxi driver.
glossary.pre-money valuation: A company's estimated value before new investment money is added.
glossary.GAAP: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the standard rules companies use when reporting their finances.
glossary.observability: Ways to tell what a running program is doing and spot when something goes wrong.
glossary.OpenTelemetry: A way to collect and send records about what software is doing, such as its requests.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.knowledge graph: A way to organize information by showing how people, places, or things are connected.
glossary.lifecycle: Rules for how long a memory stays useful and when it should expire.
glossary.conformance tests: Checks that a tool follows the agreed rules.
glossary.Peter Principle: The idea that people keep getting promoted until they reach a job they are not good at.
glossary.career pressure: The threat of losing your job or career when you can no longer move up, which can push you to take bigger risks.
glossary.imposter syndrome: The feeling that you do not deserve your success or will be found out, even when others think you are capable.
glossary.obfuscation: Making something harder to see or recognize.
glossary.coding harness: A program around a coding AI that lets it use tools like reading files and running commands.
glossary.IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an app that brings coding and other development tools together.
glossary.system prompt: Extra instructions set before a conversation that guide how the AI answers.
glossary.subagent: A helper assigned a smaller part of a larger task.
glossary.TUI: Terminal User Interface: the menus and controls an app shows inside a text terminal.
glossary.GUI: Graphical user interface: the buttons, pictures, and menus you use on a screen instead of typing commands.
glossary.natural number: A whole number used for counting, sometimes including zero.
glossary.nested square roots: A chain where you take the square root of something that already contains a square root.
glossary.base-2 logarithm: It answers: what should 2 be raised to, to make this number?
glossary.Gamma function: A function that extends the idea of factorials beyond whole numbers.
glossary.Peano arithmetic: A way to build counting numbers starting at zero and adding one again and again.
glossary.successor function: A rule that takes a number and gives the next one, like 4 becoming 5.
glossary.concatenation: Joining digits side by side to write a number, like making 22 from two 2s.
glossary.pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
glossary.merge queue: A waiting line that checks code changes before adding them to the shared project.
glossary.source control: Tools for keeping track of changes to code and helping developers work on it together.
glossary.gitignore: A rule that tells Git to leave certain files out when tracking code changes.
glossary.secret scanning: A check that looks through code for passwords or access keys.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.hidden tests: Checks kept secret from the builder, used to see whether the finished program works.
glossary.reward hacking: When an AI finds a way to get a high score without doing what its designers actually wanted.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.API key: A secret code that lets software use an online service as an approved user.
glossary.RISC-V: A processor design that sets out the basic instructions software runs on.
glossary.UART: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter: a simple connection for sending data to and from a device’s electronics.
glossary.GPIO: General-Purpose Input/Output: a pin on a small computer board that can send or read simple electrical signals.
glossary.serial bridge: A connection that lets one device pass messages between a computer and another board.
glossary.flashing: Installing replacement software directly onto a device, such as a router.
glossary.MMU: Memory Management Unit: hardware that helps an operating system manage memory and keep programs separate.
glossary.dreaming: A background pass where Claude rereads its work logs to correct or reorganize saved notes.
glossary.salience: How important something seems and whether it is worth saving for later.
glossary.wiki: A set of pages about a topic that link to related notes, helping Claude find information.
glossary.context injection: Adding extra information or instructions to what an AI sees before it responds.
glossary.microstate: A very small country that governs itself.
glossary.sovereign republic: A country that governs itself and has no monarch as its head of state.
glossary.castelli: San Marino’s name for its municipalities, or small local areas.
glossary.ecclesiastical diocese: An area of the Catholic Church overseen by a bishop.
glossary.annexation: When one country takes over a place and makes it part of its territory.
glossary.GDP: Gross Domestic Product: the total value of what a country's economy produces.
